name: Virtual Surgical Rehearsal
title: Virtual Surgical Rehearsal
answer: Virtual surgical rehearsal is the practice of planning and practicing a patient's operation on a digital or physical copy of their anatomy before entering the operating room. It covers preoperative imaging review, patient-specific model creation, step-by-step walkthroughs, and team communication for complex cases in surgical robotics and navigation. The work overlaps with surgical simulation, 3D printing, mixed reality, and computer-assisted navigation, but its defining feature is rehearsal for a specific patient rather than generic skills training. It sits within the wider field of medical AI that this site tracks across 1000 models, though not every rehearsal system uses machine learning.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Virtual surgical rehearsal is the practice of planning and practicing a patient's operation on a digital or physical copy of their anatomy before entering the operating room. It covers preoperative imaging review, patient-specific model creation, step-by-step walkthroughs, and team communication for complex cases in surgical robotics and navigation. The work overlaps with surgical simulation, 3D printing, mixed reality, and computer-assisted navigation, but its defining feature is rehearsal for a specific patient rather than generic skills training. It sits within the wider field of medical AI that this site tracks across 1000 models, though not every rehearsal system uses machine learning.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The rehearsal runs on a chain of systems that starts with diagnostic imaging such as CT or MRI and ends at a workstation, headset, or robot console. Segmentation software turns those scans into labeled anatomy, and a graphics workstation or GPU server builds and renders the patient-specific model. Physical rehearsals may use 3D printed models, while digital rehearsals may use virtual reality headsets, haptic controllers, or the same navigation and robotic interfaces used in the operating room. Data storage, network bandwidth, and display calibration matter because the rehearsal must match the planned intraoperative setup closely enough to be useful.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The usual workflow begins with image acquisition and segmentation, often with manual correction by a clinician, followed by registration of the model to the patient's anatomy or to a navigation frame. The team then simulates approaches, instrument paths, bone cuts, implant placement, or soft tissue manipulation, depending on the procedure, and reviews constraints such as reach, clearance, and access. AI may assist with segmentation, landmark detection, or path suggestion, but the surgeon and planning team remain responsible for checking the plan against the images and the patient's history. Rehearsal is iterative, so findings from one simulated attempt feed back into the next until the team agrees on a workable sequence.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Virtual surgical rehearsal depends on patient imaging and derived models, so consent, de-identification where appropriate, access control, and clear retention rules are part of the work. Provenance matters because a model may combine original scans, automated segmentation, manual edits, and third-party software, and each step should be traceable for review. Regulatory status varies by jurisdiction and by whether the output is used for planning, for navigation, or for a cleared device, and the site tracks 215 compliance and regulation pages that reflect this layered oversight. Liability questions can arise if a rehearsal model is wrong or misleading, so documentation, version control, and validation against the source images are central to safe practice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward faster and more automated segmentation, real-time model updates during surgery, and tighter coupling with robotic and navigation systems. Mixed reality and head-mounted displays may let a team rehearse in the same visual frame they will use in the operating room, while digital twin approaches aim to keep a patient-specific model current as anatomy changes. Evidence generation is likely to focus on whether rehearsal changes decisions, reduces complications, or shortens operating time, rather than on the novelty of the display alone. As these tools mature, the main constraint may be less about graphics and more about validation, data rights, and integration with existing clinical workflows.
